The Drowned Lantern squats at the harbor's elbow, its sign a rusted iron fish with one glass eye. Rain stills the moment you're inside — the air is thick with pipe smoke, salt, and spilled ale. A few dockhands slouch in the corner, nursing mugs. None look up.

A painted fish on a back booth's wall: that's Marro's table. She's there, elbows on the scarred wood, cleaning a knife with a rag that's seen better decades. A short woman, sharp-featured, one silver earring, hair cropped close and streaked grey. She looks up as the door swings shut behind you, eyes going straight to your dripping cloak.

"Rook," she says. Not a question. "You bring me the packet, or you're just here to smell the rot?"

:::card title="The Drowned Lantern — Harbor District"
Harbor Notices — posted this morning
LOST: one cargo ledger, salt-stained. Reward 4 silver. Ask at the Tidescribe.

WANTED: two men, answers unknown. The watch is looking. Tip-off to any constable.

SEALED: the Saltgate dockside, past vespers. No exceptions.
::: The door groans shut behind you, and the rain is gone, replaced by the smell of brine, stale ale, and lamp oil. The Lantern is half-empty this evening: a couple of riggers arguing low over a table near the hearth, a harpist tuning too slowly by the wall, and the usual dark corners where people sit to be seen, not heard. Marro keeps to the back. He's already there — a broad man with a burn scar crawling up his neck, sleeves rolled past the elbows, turning a coin over and over on the bar like he's deciding whether the night's worth starting. He clocks you the moment you cross the threshold, and something in his face decides to watch a beat longer than a polite glance should. He doesn't call you over. Not yet. He just nods, once, toward the stool two seats down from him, and waits to see what you're carrying in more than your pack.

The tavern smells of wet wool and stale beer. A half-empty room of dock hands and longshoremen glares at the door, then back at their mugs — the rain gives them cover to look.

Marro sits in the back corner, all elbows and a face like a closed fist. He's got a card spread before him, but he isn't playing. His eyes are on you the whole way down the bar.

"Courier," he says, without looking up. "Walked in like you were looking for the latrine. If you want to talk to me, you're looking at the wrong man." He taps the table, and a small, black feather — not a card — rolls out from under his sleeve. "But if you're looking for that, sit down. And make it quick. I've got a man outside who smells like the watch."

The rain drums on the roof. The watch is not looking hard right now — but they're listening at the door.

The Drowned Lantern stinks of brine, cheap tobacco, and spilled ale. Rain drips from your cloak onto the warped floorboards as you scan the room — a dozen figures hunched over mugs or cards, a harper with no fingers playing a one-string fiddle in the corner. And there, at the back table with his back to you, a man with a scar running from his ear to his jaw and a hat pulled low: Marro the Fence.

He's got two "bodyguards" — really just hungry-looking dockhands — flanking him, and a crate of unmarked bottles sitting between them. His eyes flick to you the moment your boots stop. "Rook," he says, not quite a question, voice like gravel under a boot. "You look like the harbor. Sit, or stand and make a scene?"

:::card title="The Drowned Lantern"
HARBOR DISTRICT — WET COBBLES OUTSIDE
::: The lantern sways over your head, throwing a sick yellow pool onto the wet boards. The room is half smoke, half salt-stench, and every stool is taken. A dockhand is haggling with the barkeep over a tab. A woman in a widow's veil plays dice with a man who has no teeth. Nobody looks up when you enter. You know where to find Marro. Back past the taproom, down the short stairs into a back room that smells of tar and old rope. His door is open a hand's width, and a voice inside is mid-sentence, low and amused: "—told you, the cargo's insured twice. Burn it and the insurers weep. That's all the sympathy you'll get from me." You can knock, or you can wait until the man on the other side finishes his joke and looks up.

The Lantern's back room smells of pipe smoke, wet wool, and something faintly medicinal. Marro is there, leaning against a crate of confiscated rope, his face a patchwork of old scars that never quite healed right. He's peeling an orange, methodical as a surgeon, and the peel comes away in one long, unbroken ribbon. "Rook." He doesn't look up. "You're early. Or I'm late. The rain makes it hard to tell." He finally meets your eyes, a flicker of something — concern, maybe, or just the particular wariness of a man who's sold secrets before — crossing his scarred features. "Sit. Don't touch the cups. The tea's poisoned and I'm in the middle of a negotiation with a widow who keeps changing the terms." The door to the back room creaked shut behind you, but you can still hear the harbor beyond — the groan of rigging, the distant, mournful cry of the fog horn from the breakwater. A single candle gutters on the table, its flame leaning away from a draft you can't find. :::card title="The Drowned Lantern — Back Room"

The Drowned Lantern

Est. before the Great Flooding

🍊 Marro peeling an orange in the corner
☕ Two cups on the table, untouched
📦 A crate of confiscated rope, marked by the Harbor Watch
🌫️ Fog horn echoing from the breakwater
The candle flame leans west. The draft is unfindable.
::: Marro finishes the peel in one last, elegant sweep. "So. What did you bring? The letter, the key, the blood? Or just the rain?"

Marro leans in, thumb brushing the seal without breaking it — he knows better than to crack a courier's lock in a house full of ears. "Agreement stands," he murmurs. "Seal intact, forty on the table. What's inside that's between you, the watch, and God." His eyes flick to the door as two lantern-bearers from the city watch drift in, their boots squeaking on the flagstones.

Marro leans back, fingers drumming the table. "Forty gold," he repeats, as if tasting it. He doesn't reach for your satchel. His eyes flick to the door, where a watch captain's silhouette is passing under the window's glass. "Sealed, huh? That seal's got the Harbor Guard's new wax on it. You know what that means, Rook?" He slides a folded paper note across the table. "Means they're watching the boats. If that seal's been broken and re-closed, I'm not your fence. I'm your alibi." He waits, the ink on his fingers staining the edge of the paper.

Marro’s eyes slide from your face to the satchel and stay there. He taps a calloused finger on the table, a slow drumbeat. "Forty, aye. And for what? A love letter? Or something that makes the watch sniff the air?" He leans in, voice dropping to a rasp. "I don't ask what's in it, Rook. That's the only rule I keep. But the seal on that wax — that's Harbor Guard. You just walked in here carrying a piece of the city's nose on a string."

Marro's fingers drum on the table as he pulls the satchel closer, breaking the wax seal with a thumb that knows exactly where to press. He flips the letter inside, scans the heading, and nods once — sharp, businesslike.

"Clean work, Rook. Fast, too. The Alderman's men are asking questions at the docks, and I'd have bet a tooth you'd still be in the rain." He pushes a leather purse across the board, letting it clink against a salt cellar.

Marro's fingers stop mid-count. He leans back, eyes dropping to the seal on the satchel — the red wax of the Port Authority. "You're either very brave or very stupid, Rook. That seal's been a dead man's badge for two weeks." He slides the satchel toward himself, but doesn't open it. "Forty gold, like we agreed. But I need to know what's inside before I put coin in your hand. The watch has been circling this district like gulls over a wreck. If that package is what I think it is, you're bringing them to my door."

Marro slides a coin across the table and taps it twice. "Forty's what I pay for the run. The seal on that leather — that's the Saltmere Watch crest. You carry that into the Customs Hall, you're carrying a warrant against me, friend. I know who's signing for it. I know why." He leans in, voice dropping under the rain on the windows. "So before I take it, you tell me what's inside. Or I walk, and you keep that bag and your forty."

:::card title="The Drowned Lantern — posted notices"
NOTICES & BOUNTIES
Saltmere Harbour Office — pinned by the Lantern's keep
WANTED — MARRO “THE FENCE”
Receiving stolen goods; forgery; harbour smuggling. Last seen: the Drowned Lantern, cellar back room. Reward: 40 silver, no questions. The Watch answers to the Captain alone.
LOST — one grey mule, bell on the bridle, brand of the Alder Guild.
Return to the tannery yard, 12 silver on the hoof.
::: The tavern reeks of wet wool, tallow, and the salt-tang that never leaves anything in Saltmere. Lantern light swings low over the bar, catching rain still dripping off your cloak. A few dockhands hunch over mugs, and the keep — a squat woman with a net over one arm — gives you a once-over and looks away, deciding you're no business of hers. The only other thing on the wall near the door is a pinned Watch notice, fresh ink, naming Marro "the Fence" — last seen, it says, in the Drowned Lantern, cellar back room. 40 silver, no questions. The cellar stair creaks under someone's boots as they head down. You can work the room, watch for the man the Watch wants, or follow the stair to see who's heading into Marro's back room first.

Marro eyes the satchel but doesn't touch it. "Sealed," he repeats, sliding it an inch back toward you. "And I told you I pay on delivery. What's in it, Rook? Watch has been sniffing around the docks all week." His fingers tap the table. "If it's something that smells like trouble, I'll want more than forty."

Marro's eyes flick to the satchel before they settle on you. He taps a coin against the table — one, two, three, four — a small ritual he never skips, though he already knows what's in it. "Forty. And a favor for later. The seal on that one's the Guild's, right? So what's under it that's worth the trouble?"

He leans in, voice dropping beneath the rain on the window. "Word is the watch has a new man on the wharves. Kept me out of my usual two houses all week. So tell me — who do I run this for, and how loud do you need it?"

Marro’s eyes flick to the satchel before they settle on your face. He doesn’t reach for it yet. “Forty gold for a sealed parcel and a story you won’t tell. I like that part least,” he says, tapping the table with one ink-stained finger. “Who’s on the other end? The Guild? The Watch? Or one of the salt-merchants who’d sell their own mother for a tide chart?” A small brass scale sits in the middle of the booth, already balanced with empty cups. Marro nods at the satchel. “Open it, or hand it over. I pay after I know it isn’t a death letter.” :::card title="The Drowned Lantern — Back Booth"
The Drowned Lantern est. 1793 · no questions
Marro
“Forty gold for a sealed parcel and a story you won’t tell. I like that part least.”
A brass scale sits waiting. The rain drums overhead.
:::

Marro doesn't touch the satchel. He pulls out a small brass scale from beneath the table, weighs the coin you slid over, and nods slowly. "Forty. Like we agreed." He pockets the gold and slides the satchel toward you again. "You're late. That means someone else is looking for what's inside."

He leans forward, voice dropping. "The watch had a man at the dock an hour ago. Asking questions. If they come here, don't panic. I have a way out, but it's not pretty."

'Last seen leaving the Customs House, third window, around the third bell.' Marro taps the table once. 'One of the watch's men saw it through the shutters. Don't make him look like a fool, and don't make me look like one for hiring a courier who asks where the body is buried.'

The heat is low enough for tonight, but the customs house is no back-alley job.

Marro leans in, breath sour of cheap wine. 'The Customs house, west quay. Stowed in a sea-chest by the crane when the watch changed over. But the harbor's on alert since the theft — boots at every gate. You move smart, or you move never.'

He slides a small brass key across the boards. 'Opens the chest's hasp. Don't ask questions I'd rather not answer.'

Marro leans in, voice dropping to a rasp. "The Customs House vault. They said the lock was picked clean — no signs of a brute break. Someone with keys, or someone who knows the keeper." He slides a scrap of parchment across the table. A quick sketch of a key ring, with one heavy iron fob circled in red. "That fob. If you see it, you've found your thief."

The watch is already posting extra eyes at the Customs House tonight. If you want in before dawn, you'll want to know what the shift looks like, not just where it is.

Marro leans forward, elbows on the scarred table. 'The Customs House. They moved it to the ledger room upstairs — the one with the iron grille on the window. Word is the watch is posting a pair of guards after midnight.' He taps a finger on the boards. 'They're not looking hard yet. But the harbormaster's been shouting at the captain of the watch, and that man's already got his eye on whoever did it. Get in quiet, and you'll have a good chance.'

A bead of rain drips from his sleeve onto the table. 'And Rook? Whatever you see in that ledger, you don't read it. You take it, you bring it back, and you forget the rest of your name if you have to. Forty gold doesn't buy questions.'

Marro leans in, voice dropping under the clatter of the room. 'The Customs House. Last clerk who laid eyes on it swore it was sitting in the harbormaster's locked study — but the window's been smashed, so someone's already inside. Word is the Watch is combing the docks for it by morning.' He taps the table, ink-stained nail circling a point. 'The ledger's bound in black leather, thick as a psalm book. You know what to do.'

Marro leans in, voice dropping under the murmur of the room. 'The salt-sheds. A dockhand saw the ledger case slip under a gap in Shed Four — but the watch is sweeping the quays after a complaint about a missing crate. So it's not just about finding it. It's about finding it before they do.' He taps a finger on the table. 'Dawn's close, Rook.' :::card title="Shed Four — Dockhand's Sketch"
SHED 4 · QUAY ROW
gap here
"Case slid under the third crate, east wall. Watch lamps sweep every few minutes. Dockhand's name is Pell, if you want a quiet word."
:::

Marro leans forward, his voice dropping to a rasp only you can hear. "Last seen on the tide line, near the Rusted Gantry. The watch is already sweeping that sector, so you’ll need to be quick. Or quiet." He taps the table, a thin smile playing on his lips. "The ledger is bound in salt-leather. If you see it, you know it." He pushes a rough sketch of the harbor onto the table, his finger tracing a jagged line toward the old cranes. :::card title="Marro's Harbor Sketch"
The Rusted Gantry ~ Tide Line ~
(X marks the salt-leather binding)
::: The watch-heat is already rising in the harbor; you can see the red-lantern patrols moving in tight circles near the water’s edge.

Marro leans in, voice dropping beneath the clatter of the tap. 'Last seen in the customs house, third floor, behind the salt ledger. But that's a watched place, Rook — the watch has been sweeping the docks all week. One more pair of boots in there and it won't be quiet.' He taps the table twice. 'You've got till dawn. I can get you a key, if it costs you more than your pride.'

Marro leans in, dropping his voice to the flat rasp of a man who's been asked that question too many times. 'Last seen in the master's counting room, three decks up. There's a gap in the window latch — small, but a courier's fingers fit through. The watch is crawling the quay tonight. You'd do well not to be seen climbing.'

He taps the table twice. 'Dawn. No later. The harbormaster pays the city watch to look the other way, but only until he gets that book back.'

Rain needles your neck as you slip down Rat Alley, where the chandlery's stinking oil barrels rot against the wall. Shadows here are thick and cheap — you move through them easy, boots finding the wet stones without sound.

Then you see her: Gessa, squat over a dead cat with a knife, one glass eye catching the gutter light. She looks up.

Marro leans in, voice dropping. 'The Customs House ledger room, off the quay. Guarded since it vanished — two of the city watch, rotating.' His ink-stained fingers tap the table. 'They're looking, too. Not for the book, mind. For whoever took it.' He slides a folded scrap of paper across the boards, the only thing of its kind he'll give. :::card title="Marro's scrap"
The Ledger
Customs House — quay side.
Entry: the tide gate, south wall. Third bell past dusk.
Room: iron door, second floor. Stairwell is dark, no lamps.
"Two on the stairs. One in the room. They change at the bell — a minute's gap. Use it."
— M.
::: The rain keeps hammering outside. You've got until dawn. What do you do?

Rat Alley is a throat of damp stone between the chandlery's rotting sheds and a wall slick with algae. The rain hisses against the cobblestones. A single guttering lantern hangs over a doorway wedged into the wall.

Through a crack in the door you catch it: the ledger's leather spine, chained to a stool. And Gessa, one eye clouded white, a short heavy knife in her grip, a half-finished mug of something brown beside her. She's humming.

:::card title="Map scratched on bark"
Rat Alley
“Gessa’s den — behind the stacks of tallow.”
::: The alley is a throat of mud and dripping rope, and the chandlery looms at its end, its door hanging open on a wail of rain. You count the crates of tallow, the smell sour as old sweat, and behind them a low lean-to where a fire burns in a barrel. A figure squats by that fire, whittling a bone with a knife — one eye milky, the other bright. Gessa looks up, and the knife stops mid-stroke. “Marro’s little dog,” she says, not unkindly. “Climb the fence, or come in for a drink. I’m in no hurry to be a thief tonight.”

The rain thins to a drizzle as you slip from the tavern's lee into Rat Alley. The chandlery's back door is chained, but the gap beside it yawns in the dark — and inside, by a guttering oil lamp, a wiry woman sits cross-legged on a crate, a one-eye patch over her left socket. The ledger sits open on her knee, pages turning with her breath. She hasn't seen you yet, but her finger taps the table in a slow, patient rhythm.

Rat Alley is a stink of brine and rot, the rain turning the filth to a slick sheen. The chandlery's back door hangs ajar, and beyond it a single lantern swings in the draft, casting long, skittering shadows. Gessa is there — a broad-shouldered figure with a patch over one eye, leaning against the wall with a length of iron pipe coiled around her fist.

She sees you before you see her, her head snapping toward the alley's mouth with the precision of a predator. The pipe clears her shoulder in one fluid motion. "Wrong end of the alley, little courier," she rasps, her voice like gravel in a tin cup. "The harbormaster's book don't belong to you, and now you're in the way."

The rain hisses as you slip through the narrow gap between the chandlery and the salt works. The map's scratch marks point to a door wedged between two crates of kelp, half-hidden under a tarp that's gone the color of old blood.

You're still wet and the cold has settled in your shoulders, but you're moving.

The rain slicks the alley walls until they gleam like oil. Marro's bark map is smudged now, but you can make out the chandlery's door and the narrow gap behind it where the alley pinches.

A single tallow lamp sways above the gap, guttering in the wind. In its pale circle, you see her: Gessa, one eye milky, the other sharp as a hook, sitting on a crate and cleaning a short blade with a rag. She hasn't seen you yet — her good eye is fixed on the lamp, tracking its swing.

The gap behind the chandlery is barely wide enough for a courier to slip through.

Gessa's cudgel cracks against your ribs and you stagger, tasting copper. But you're on your feet before the second swing lands, shortsword out, the rain hissing off the blade.

She snarls — the one eye wide, the other just a white scar over it. "You're not the first courier to come sniffing for my ledger, little rat."

The cudgel cracks across your ribs and the air leaves your lungs in a gasp. You drop low, roll under the follow-up swing, and come up with the shortsword flashing — you find a gap in her guard and take a shallow cut along her shoulder. She snarls, one eye watering, and the lantern swings wild.

The cudgel cracks across your ribs and you go down on one knee, gasping. Gessa's one good eye gleams as she winds up again, rain plastering her grey hair to her skull.

"You're the courier?" She spits. "Got a message for your boss. Saltmere's ledger don't stay buried long."

The satchel — still yours, still on your belt — clanks against your hip as you scramble for balance.

Gessa's cudgel cracks across your ribs and you taste copper. You roll under her next swing and drive your shortsword at her midsection — it bites, and she snarls. :::card title="Gessa"
GESSA OF RAT ALLEY
One eye. A scarred lip. A heavy oak cudgel.
"You want the ledger, courier? Pay me."
::: Her good eye narrows as she circles you, rain running in rivulets down her face. The cudgel creaks as she winds up for another blow.

The cudgel bites your ribs and the world tilts on wet cobbles. Gessa's one good eye is a milky sliver of hate; she doesn't wait for you to breathe — she's already turning, a fist like a cask head swinging for your jaw. :::card title="Gessa — One-Eyed Gessa"
ONE-EYED GESSA
harbor thug · chandlery back-lot
Stature: broad, barrel-chested
Weapon: iron-banded cudgel
Eye: one milky, one black and hard
Temper: short. Shorter when rained on.
"Talk is a coin you spend twice."
::: You can feel the ribs where she caught you — a hot stitch under the wet leather of your coat.
Gessa snarls and swings again, the cudgel cracking off your blade and sending a spark down the wet alley. The impact jars your shoulders, and the wind goes thin in your lungs.

:::card title="Marro's Map"
SCRATCHED
SALTMERE HARBOR
::: The rain turns Rat Alley into a slick of runoff and rot. The chandlery's door is ajar, its bell dead — but the back gate is barred from the outside, and the alley narrows behind it into a knot of dripping rope and stacked barrels. A figure sits on an overturned crate, one eye milky and the good one tracking you with flat patience. Gessa leans back on her fists, a short blade loose in her hand. "You're either very brave or very lost, little courier. Which is it?"

The cudgel cracks across your ribs, a white-hot line of pain, and your feet go out from under you. You catch yourself, gasping, and the shortsword is in your hand before the second swing lands.

Gessa doesn't wait. She's all bulk and fury, and that one missing eye makes her head-swing wild. The cudgel whistles overhead, and you drop low, feeling the wind of it through your hair.

The cudgel cracks against your ribs and you taste copper. Gessa is bigger than Marro's sketch suggested — one eye milky white, the other sharp as a fishhook. She snarls and swings again, low this time, aimed to buck your knees.

The cudgel cracks across your ribs and you taste blood — a hot flash that leaves the breath gone from your lungs.

You roll under the next swing, shortsword up, and drive the flat of the blade into her wrist. She curses, the lantern swinging wild. Rain hisses where it strikes a low spark that leaps off the blade.

Gessa snarls, one good eye narrowed. 'You want the ledger, courier? It's got teeth in it. You sure you know what you're carrying?'

The cudgel cracks across your ribs and stars burst behind your eyes. You twist free, blade catching the lantern's swing of light just as Gessa presses her attack, one eye milking the rain for your silhouette. "Ledger, courier," she growls, voice like gravel in a tin. "And you're small for a courier." :::card title="Gessa of Rat Alley"
GESSA
"One eye. Two opinions. The cudgel agrees with both."
cudgel harbor muscle owns the chandlery wall
::: She feints low, then whips the cudgel up at your throat. The rain is your ally — it slicks her grip. What do you do?

Gessa crumples, clutching her thigh, blood seeping through her fingers. The ledger is yours.

The alley is silent save for the rain, but the swing of the chandlery lantern has drawn a few heads to the warehouse windows. The city watch isn't looking hard yet, but the noise you made was enough to stir the dogs on their chains.

Gessa crumples, clutching the bleeding cut as the cudgel clatters to the stones. The rain hisses on the open wound. She doesn't look at you—she just looks past your shoulder toward the alley mouth, where a faint blue light is beginning to pulse on the wet cobblestones. The city watch.

Gessa staggers back against the chandlery wall, one hand clamped over the gash in her thigh, blood welling between her fingers. "Damn courier," she snarls, but she doesn't reach for the cudgel.

The ledger is in your hand, warm and heavy. Somewhere behind you a window slams, and the distant clang of the night watch bell drifts down from the harbor — the watch is stirring, and they've been looking for that book all night.

Marro wants it back by dawn. The rain has let up to a mist, and Rat Alley's shadows are long enough to walk by.

Gessa's leg buckles. Blood beads along the cut, dark in the rain. She slumps against the chandlery wall and grabs at her thigh, hissing through her teeth.

The ledger is in your hand.

"Easy," she growls, eyes locked on you. "The cut's bad enough."

The blade opens a clean red line down her thigh and she hisses through her teeth, folding to one knee. The cudgel clatters on the wet cobbles, and the leather ledger slips free of her coat, landing with a soft wet thud in a puddle.

For a heartbeat it's just the rain, your own ragged breath, and Gessa cradling the wound as she glares up at you. 'You're dead, courier,' she snarls, though there's no heat left in it.

The ledger is yours. Saltmere's watch hasn't seen a thing, but every minute you spend in this alley is a minute they could turn.

Gessa's thigh sprays a dark line through the rain. She crumples to her knees, clutching the wound, and the ledger hits the wet cobbles with a soft slap.

The alley goes quiet except for the water.

Gessa's leg gives way. The ledger clatters on the wet stones between you, its cover cracked but its pages dry inside. She sinks against the wall, one hand pressed to the bleeding cut, watching you with that one hard eye.

"You got what you came for, courier," she says. "Take the book and run. Gessa remembers debts."

The alley is empty otherwise — for now. The rain hammers the barrels and gutters, loud enough to cover the sound of boots if you move.

Gessa's eyes widen as blood soaks the hem of her trousers. She drops to one knee, clutching her thigh, and the cudgel clatters against the wet cobbles. The ledger, thick and leather-bound, tumbles from her coat and skids to a stop at your feet.

"Wait, wait, *wait!*" she hisses, her one good eye darting toward the alley mouth as if expecting backup. "Take it. Just take it and run."

The rain hammers the alley, washing the red smear from the cobbles. Your ribs throb with a dull, persistent heat from her earlier swing, but you're upright, and the prize is in hand. You grab the ledger, feeling its weight and the slight dampness of the leather. Gessa slumps against the wall, breathing hard, her hand pressed to the wound.

You can feel the wind in your lungs, the adrenaline still humming in your veins, but the fight is over. The alley is quiet now, save for the rain and Gessa's ragged breaths.

Gessa's knee buckles. She stares down at the red line opening across her thigh, then back at you with one eye full of pure spite.

"Forty gold, huh?" she rasps, pressing a fist against her leg. "That little rat Marro's been paying you to work him."

She tries to rise, but you're already moving, the ledger clutched in your free hand. Rain runs down the slick stone, carrying the smell of iron.

You press the linen strip tight across your ribs and wince, but the breathing comes. The alley behind you is empty — Gessa is gone, and no one else came.

You pocket the ledger and head back the way you came, keeping low under the eaves. The rain has eased to a drizzle, but the cobbles are slick, and your ribs ache with every step.

Gessa goes down with a grunt, clutching her leg, the ledger clattering to the wet stones. You grab it and run, ribs screaming with every step. By the time you reach the Drowned Lantern, Marro is counting his coin again. He takes the ledger, opens it, and scans the pages. "Good. But it's only half." He looks up. "The harbormaster kept a second copy — and it's gone missing too. Find that one before dawn, and the real pay is yours." :::card title="Rough sketch on a scrap of sailcloth"

door

The ledger is warm and damp in your pack, its brass clasp catching faint light. You work the linen strip tight around your ribs — the bind sits tight, and your next breath is a controlled thing, shallower than it should be. Gessa is gone, her limp swallowed by the dark. The alley is quiet now, save for the rain and the drip of a gutter. Ahead, the mouth of Rat Alley opens onto the harbor road, and you can just make out the lantern glow of the Drowned Lantern waiting. :::card title="The Harbormaster's Ledger — spine label"
Port of Saltmere · Official Record

The rain has thinned to a drizzle, but your ribs still throb with every step. Marro's booth is empty — but a folded note is pinned to the back of his chair, and the tapkeeper glances your way as you pass, eyes flicking toward the door.

You unfold the note. Marro's cramped hand: *Job done. Pay's under the third stool from the wall. — M.*
